# Benchmarks

> **This file is generated by robots.** [`bench/benchmark.test.ts`](bench/benchmark.test.ts) measures the API under load and writes this file, whole, each time it runs. Don't edit it by hand, as the next run replaces whatever is here: to change what it says, change the benchmark and run it again.

## What was measured

- **When:** 2026-11-16 01:13 UTC. 177,255 requests were counted.
- **Code:** Evieverse 0.1.0, commit `aa2eb1c` with uncommitted changes to the server.
- **Server:** one process, in a container that may use 2 CPUs and 2 GB of memory, with no swap (Linux 6.10.14-linuxkit, Node v22.23.5). The most it used over a load was 1.98 CPUs, and the most memory it held at any time was 403 MB. It runs from source, as `npm run dev` runs it, with every setting at its [default](docs/CONFIG.md): SQLite in a file, content and summaries in a directory, the feed index in the process's memory, and the compactor running in the same process. Its files are on a Docker volume, which took 0.91 ms to flush a small file. It logs every request, as a server does, to nowhere. Four settings differ, without which there would be no load to measure: users post and comment as often as they like (`POST_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=0`, `COMMENTS_PER_MINUTE=0`), and are never asked to solve a challenge for a post or a comment (`CHALLENGE_POST_WINDOW_SECONDS=0`, `CHALLENGE_COMMENTS_PER_MINUTE=0`).
- **Data:** 2,000 posts under 39 hashtags by 626 users, spread over the last 30 days with the newest days the fullest, with 8,679 likes and 500 comments. They are the [testbed](testbed)'s made-up posts, and the same on every run.
- **Load:** 50 HTTP connections from a second container, over Docker's network, opened before a load starts and kept open, each sending its next request as soon as its last is answered, for 10 seconds a load, after 2 seconds of the same requests that aren't counted. Every request says it takes compressed responses (`Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br`), as a browser's does. The connections belong to 4 threads, and their container has 4 CPUs of its own, so sending requests takes none of the server's.
- **Machine:** Intel(R) Xeon(R) W-2140B CPU @ 3.20GHz, 16 cores, 32 GB of memory, Darwin 24.6.0 (x64). Its load average was 2.9 when the run started, so it had other work to do at the same time. Docker 27.4.0 (Docker Desktop) runs both containers, and has 16 of the machine's CPUs and 7.7 GB of its memory to run them with.

## Results

Times are from sending a request to the end of its response. *p50*, *p90* and *p99* are the times that 50%, 90% and 99% of requests were answered within. *CPUs* is the CPU time the server's process used for each second of the load, its warm-up included: 1.00 is one CPU busy throughout, and it may use 2 CPUs. *Memory* is the memory the process held when the load ended, of the 2 GB it may use. *Response* is the average size of a response's body as it was sent, which is compressed where the server compresses it. Every request was answered, with the response expected: a run in which one isn't fails, and writes no file.

## Reading the numbers

- **They are those of a server with 2 CPUs and 2 GB of memory, on one machine.** The limits say what the server had, and keep the rest of the machine out of its reach. They don't make this machine's CPUs or its disk another's: compare a run with another on the same machine, not with this file.
- **They are a single process's,** on SQLite and a local disk. A server answers requests on one thread, and uses others to read and write files and to compress: the *CPUs* column is how much of its CPUs it had a use for. A deployment with several nodes, Postgres or MySQL, Redis and an object store ([DEPLOY.md](docs/DEPLOY.md)) has other limits, which this doesn't measure.
- **The network is Docker's.** The requests come from a container on the same machine as the server's, so there is no distance in the times.
- **Requests a second are the most the server answered,** not a rate it was sent: a connection waits for its answer before it sends again. So more connections get more out of the server only until it is busy, and past that each request waits longer. [More connections](#more-connections) shows where that is for the mix.
- **The connections were already open.** Each load's connections are opened first, while the server has nothing else to do, so the times above have no connecting in them. A server that is busy takes new connections slowly, so clients that keep their connections open get these numbers, and ones that connect for every request to a busy server don't.
- **Writes are flushed to the disk.** A post is three files in the content store (its bytes, its summary and its meta file) and a comment is one, and each is flushed to the disk before the request is answered. So a write has two things to wait for, and the numbers say which it was: how long the server's disk took to flush a file is under [What was measured](#what-was-measured), and a write whose *CPUs* are close to 2 had every CPU the server may use busy: it was those it waited for, more than the disk.
- **Writes reach feeds later.** A post or a like is answered once it is stored; the compactor puts it in feeds within a few seconds, and its work is part of what the server was doing during every load here.
